extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and newspaper reporters (those who write police/crime news)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting and writing police news and crime stories for newspapers, covering selection of story type, ethical purpose, treatment, fairness, and the specific facts to include.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of story / appropriate treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Since police news ranges from slight misdemeanors to the most serious of crimes ... it offers widely different material for news stories. Because of the general interest in the material with which stories of crime deal, the purely informative story is sufficient in itself to insure reading. The strong personal element in stories of wrong-doing gives occasion for effective human interest presentation in the informative story. Amusing aspects of minor offenses ... often furnish inspiration for humorous treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the story type and tone according to the material: purely informative for many crime items; human-interest emphasis when a strong personal element exists; humorous treatment may be appropriate for amusing aspects of minor offenses. (Examples referenced: burglary, forgery, intoxication, hold-up.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the effect on the reader (purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: In no other kind of news should the effect of the story on the reader receive more careful consideration than in news of crime. The evil effects of news stories of criminal acts on many readers have already been pointed out. That these destructive influences can be offset to a considerable extent by constructive handling of news has also been shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for constructive handling so the story can deter wrongdoing: show that the crime is wrong; emphasize legal penalties, remorse, guilty conscience, and disgrace brought to others; make the consequences clear to readers so the story tends to deter others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize underlying causes and responsibility (constructive presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive presentation of crime news may also include emphasis on underlying causes and responsibility, especially when these can be traced to bad conditions in the community or in society as a whole, since such emphasis leads readers to consider the necessity for changing the conditions that are directly or indirectly responsible for the criminal acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, investigate and report causes, motives, and social or community conditions tied to the crime; use such emphasis to encourage public consideration of preventive or remedial measures. If the criminal is a victim of circumstances, sympathetic understanding may be legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating sympathy for undeserving wrong-doer / avoid sentimental treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A danger in writing stories of crime lies in creating sympathy for the undeserving wrong-doer by a sentimental treatment of him and his act. By making more or less of a hero of him, news stories may lead undiscriminating readers to regard him and his crime as not unworthy of emulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not glamourize or sentimentalize criminals or their acts; avoid treatments that might make crimes seem admirable or worth emulating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not sacrifice truth or accuracy for picturesqueness or drama
rubrics_metrics.description: There is also a temptation in writing crime stories to sacrifice truth and accuracy of detail in order to secure greater picturesqueness or stronger dramatic situations, but such treatment is an indefensible deviation from the fundamental duty of presenting the news fairly and accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters must preserve factual accuracy even when dramatic color or vividness is tempting; never alter or invent details to heighten drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid moralizing or editorializing; let facts produce influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever influence a story of crime may have on the reader should be the result of the reporter's selection and presentation of the actual facts. Moralizing or 'editorializing' concerning the facts is not only unnecessary but undesirable in news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present facts neutrally and let the facts speak; refrain from inserting overt moral judgments or editorial commentary in crime news copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment: use dramatic narrative and vivid description when true to the facts; maintain single point of view; use available material
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic narrative and vivid description, when true to the facts of the news, are both legitimate and commendable. It is important to keep consistently to one point of view in arranging and presenting the details, particularly in constructive stories. Available material for making the narration and the description effective includes confessions, interviews with witnesses and persons involved, and clues to the identity of the perpetrator or to the solution of any mysterious phases of the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative and description to make the story effective only insofar as they are supported by facts. Structure the account around a consistent point of view. Employ confessions, witness interviews, and clues to enrich the narrative and help explain the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness to accused persons; right of reply and cautious language until conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairness requires that persons accused of wrong-doing as well as their accusers be given a hearing in news stories. It must also be remembered that a person accused of crime is not a criminal unless he has been convicted; until he has been found guilty, he is described as an 'alleged' criminal, or is said to be 'charged' with the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give accused persons opportunity to respond; include their side where possible; qualify descriptions (use 'alleged', 'charged') until legal conviction to avoid prejudicing readers and to preserve fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents: details of significance to include in police/crime stories
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) number of lives destroyed or endangered; (2) names of victims; (3) names of persons charged with the crime; (4) arrests of suspects and detention of witnesses; (5) clues to the identity of the perpetrators when these are not known; (6) causes, motives, and responsibility, known or conjectured; (7) amount and character of loss; (8) methods employed in commission of the crime; (9) measures to prevent similar crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the story covers these elements as relevant; they provide the substantive facts readers expect and help to explain significance, culpability, consequences, and potential prevention.
